audit.recode_to: no lexical/obligatory word stress (tone language; sporadic expressive stress, which when present falls on the first syllable) -- or, if the scheme has no such class, keep 'initial' but drop strict/dominant and add a caution flag 'expressive, non-obligatory (Samarin 1963:1, 28)'
audit.reasoning: Sourcing itself is solid: the deciding text is Samarin's reference grammar (1963 typescript = 1967 Mouton), held in full with a text layer, and both quoted passages are verbatim at p.1 and §3.30 p.28 (PDF p.54). The risk is in the reading, not the source. Samarin files stress under Intonation, says twice that it is 'not a significant feature of the phonemic structure', 'not lexically significant', 'used expressively', and that 'it is difficult to determine why stress sometimes occurs at all'; the initial-syllable statement describes where this optional expressive prominence lands when it occurs. His 1967 Basic Course (fetched sources now, ERIC ED018784) instructs learners to avoid stressing any syllable and explains that English speakers mis-hear high tone as stress; his 2013 APiCS sketch (fetched sources now) describes three tone levels and never mentions stress. Coding Sango as 'fixed-strict, dominant

sources.quote: §3.24: pitch levels 'are determined in part by the contiguous tones, by position in the sentence, by stress, by the emotional state of the speaker'; monotony drill: 'Avoid stressing one syllable more than the others.' Lesson 8: 'The native speaker of English will be inclined to stress the first or second syllables of polysyllabic Sango words ... because he interprets the syllables with high tone as having the main stress ... Listen to the following words and mimic the tones, making a special point of not adding stress to the syllables.'

sources.quote: 'Sango has three levels of pitch, as does Ngbandi ... Pitch features in only a few words to differentiate lexemes and has very little role in grammar ... Questions are not ordinarily marked by a special feature of pitch, but when a question is repeated or when expressing emotion, a rising-falling contour with greater emphasis occurs on the final syllable.' No mention of word stress anywhere in the chapter.
